bib.title: The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 2nd ed., Chapter 8: Human Resources Management

question: How should HR data, whose facts are mostly non-numeric and constantly changing, be modelled dimensionally?
contributions: Time-stamped type 2 employee transaction dimension replacing a factless transaction fact table
Periodic snapshot fact keyed to the month-end employee transaction row
Audit dimension for lineage and data-quality metadata
Skills keyword outrigger and delimited-list outrigger for multivalued attributes

results.claim: A time-stamped employee transaction dimension holding 100,000 employees at 10 transactions each per year stays small.
results.metric: raw size of employee transaction dimension
results.setup: 100,000 employees, 10 HR profile transactions per employee per year, 2,000-byte rows, 5 years
results.quote: 5 years of profile data only adds up to 10 GB (5 years x 100,000 employees x 2,000 bytes x 10 transactions per year) of raw data

limits: No measurements; sizing is a single back-of-envelope example.
Leading-wildcard LIKE searches on the delimited skills list are conceded to be slow when the dimension is large.
Written in 2002; the expiration-date-in-far-future advice and SQL (UNION/INTERSECTION, pattern indexes) reflect that era's engines.
practices: Do not keep a factless transaction fact table whose row count equals a type 2 dimension's; fold the transaction into the dimension (p.188-189).
Give each transaction-dimension row its own surrogate key, not a smart key of employee ID, code and date (p.189).
Store transaction effective and expiration date/times on each row so the dimension can be time-sliced alone; constrain date >= effective and < expiration (p.190).
Set the current row's expiration to an arbitrary far-future date rather than null, to keep queries simple (p.190).
Add a most-recent-transaction indicator and update the prior row when a new transaction arrives (p.190).
Collapse source-system microtransactions into one supertransaction (e.g. promotion), ideally from a high-level action field in the HR application (p.191).
Put numeric attributes that are summed in a fact table; ones only constrained on stay in the dimension (p.189).
In a monthly periodic snapshot, use the employee transaction key effective on the last day of the month; treat balances as semiadditive, averaged over time (p.192).

Add one audit foreign key to fact tables carrying source system, extract software version, allocation logic version, null reason, post-load alteration and outlier flags, as textual decodes (p.193-194).
For multivalued skills, use a skills group outrigger; OR queries are simple, AND needs UNION/INTERSECTION SQL hidden behind an interface (p.195-196).
Alternatively use one delimited string per skills list (e.g. \Unix\C++\) and LIKE '%\UNIX\%' so AND/OR are single SELECTs; normalise case; pin in memory or use a pattern index if slow (p.196).
Model surveys as one fact row per question per respondent, with role-playing responding and reviewed employee dimensions plus survey, question and response category dimensions (p.197-198).

terms.definition: Adding effective and expiration date/time stamps, along with a transaction description, on each row can embellish the design of a type 2 slowly changing dimension to allow very precise time slicing of the dimension by itself.
A dimension referenced by a single audit foreign key in a fact table, making data staging lineage and confidence metadata regular queryable data.
A dimension joined to the employee dimension where one group key maps to one row per keyword skill, handling a variable number of skills.
A single warehouse transaction (e.g. employee promotion) encapsulating many source-system microtransactions.
A balance, which must be averaged across the time dimension after adding across the other dimensions.
